articles.title_zh: U.S. Treasury yields tick higher as global bond rout slows
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields inched higher on Friday as recent selling pressure intensified following hawkish Fed commentary and stronger-than-expected economic data.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note was up less than one basis point to 5.17%, after reaching its highest rate since June 2007 on Thursday. The 30-year Treasury bond was flat at 5.463%, after surging to levels not seen since 2004. The 2-year note yield was also little changed at 4.899%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Investors weighed a global bond selloff this week as Japanese government bonds, U.K. gilts, German bunds and other eurozone bonds hit fresh highs. Eurozone and Japanese government bond yields edged lower on Friday.
Treasury yields have been driven higher by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, who said in a speech on Wednesday that "further policy adjustments" can be expected to bring inflation down to target. Other factors included stubbornly high oil prices and the purchasing managers' index report hitting its highest level in more than four years.
Traders were last pricing in a nearly 71% chance of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
On Friday, investors will watch the University of Michigan consumer sentiment report and durable goods data.
"Ahead, we think that there are enough rate hike fears discounted at this juncture, and certainly enough to take care of perceived inflation risks," ING's regional head of research for the Americas Padhraic Garvey and senior rates strategist Benjamin Schroeder wrote in a note on Friday.
"But, government bond yields are primed to remain under pressure on a pure debt dynamic theory, which translates into pressure for some re-widening in swap spreads, and especially in the 10yr area."
"So far, Treasury Secretary Bessent's buyback programme has in fact been successful in the sense that it was followed up by tighter swap spreads."

articles.title_zh: New Jersey Gov. Sherrill calls on her lieutenant governor to resign
articles.content_orig:
Mikie Sherrill says Dale Caldwell ‘engaged in serious, repeated violations’ involving staffers and gifts
New Jersey’s governor on Thursday called on the state’s lieutenant governor, Dale Caldwell, to resign by Friday after a law firm hired by her office concluded he violated the state’s ethics and discrimination rules.
The report published Wednesday found that Caldwell violated the state’s policy prohibiting discrimination in the workplace. It said he made an advance toward a staffer’s friend and when he was rebuffed, he told the staffer: “You young women are looking for young sperm.”
“The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office,” Mikie Sherrill, the governor, said in a statement.
Caldwell’s lawyer, Thomas Calcagni, disputed the allegations, calling the investigation a one-sided operation that did not include necessary due process.
“The Lieutenant Governor was not provided a meaningful opportunity to address each of these anonymous allegations,” he said in a statement.
The report also accused Caldwell of breaking the state’s ethics rules by trying to get a promotion for a state employee he was dating and by bringing his personal guests to ticketed events without paying for them.
“Where a sponsor waives admission to an event for an official’s family member, friend, or date, the value of that admission is an impermissible benefit to the official,” the report said.
Sherrill, a Democrat, said Caldwell’s “ethical lapses” continued even with multiple warnings and trainings. She called his resignation “in the best interest of New Jersey residents”.
“These violations substantiated in the investigation reflect a pattern of behavior that does not meet the standards of this Administration,” she said.

articles.content_orig:
Trump likely shrugged off Pezeshkian UN attack as he 'holds the cards,' foreign policy expert says.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital Wednesday.
The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of one another, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount.
"Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu , a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian holds a picture, which he says is from the Minab school that was hit by an airstrike, as he addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. headquarters Sept. 23, 2026, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us."
"I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record.
Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faces a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday.
While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
President Donald Trump addresses the UNGA in New York City. (Michael Santiago/Getty Images)
"To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said.
"Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now."
Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes.
Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive.
Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and President Donald Trump (Majid Saeedi/Getty Images; Jose Luis Magana/AP)
Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other."
But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework.
"It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said.
"In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic."
The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict.
TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters Sept. 23, 2026, in New York City. (Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images)
"Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said.
Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy .
"I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program.
"Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved.

"Of course, the Trump administration is looking for a political win here."
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: CNN, MS NOW White House reporters denied access to Xi’s state dinner arrival
articles.title_zh: CNN, MS NOW White House reporters denied access to Xi’s state dinner arrival
articles.content_orig:
Officials deny entry even after federal judge rules Trump administration must grant banned journalists access
Journalists for CNN and MS Now were denied access to the White House state dinner in honor of Xi Jinping, China’s president, on Thursday evening, hours after a federal judge ruled the Trump administration must allow them in after imposing a ban last week.
“About an hour before Xi’s arrival was scheduled, the White House said CNN could cover the event, but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, notably excluding the network’s editorial team consisting of a reporter and producer,” CNN reported .
MS Now, another outlet banned from the White House by Trump last week for what he calls overly negative coverage of his presidency, also said its White House reporter, Laura Barrón-López, was prevented from covering Xi’s arrival for the state dinner despite applying for credentials to cover the event. When Barrón-López asked a White House staffer why she was denied access, the staffer said she should “talk to Steven”, apparently meaning White House communications director Steven Cheung, MS Now reported.
Xi’s arrival for the dinner, with his wife, Peng Liyuan, was streamed live on YouTube by the White House, but none of the major US networks provided live broadcast video of the event in solidarity with CNN , a member of the broadcast pool.
Earlier on Thursday, journalists for CNN, MS Now and Politico, which was also part of the ban issued last week, were finally granted access to the White House after days of being barred from the building.
Earlier attempts by the journalists to enter the building had been unsuccessful, and lawyers representing the three organizations had told a judge that the White House has already “repeatedly violated” his overnight order requiring the Trump administration to return the press badges of journalists from the three news organizations.
Timothy Kelly, the US district judge who appeared skeptical of arguments from lawyers representing the White House during a hearing on Wednesday, issued an early morning order forcing the administration to return access for a 14-day period.
But journalists from the three affected networks reported being barred from the building, with some having their badges taken for the first time.
“This morning journalists from each of CNN, MS Now, and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated,” lawyers for the three news organizations wrote in a brief requesting a video or telephone conference “as soon as possible this morning”.
In a legal filing on Thursday afternoon, Micah Stopperich, the White House director of press operations, said in a sworn statement that the operations team was notified at 7.10am to restore access, and that it began reinstating badges at 7.25am. She said that US Secret Service indicated that badges were re-activated as of 9.07am, and that confiscated badges were dropped off at the entry to the building just before 10am.
“United States Secret Service has represented that press passes that were turned on were available for pick up at the press gate as soon as they were delivered,” she said.
The badges were revoked on Saturday, after the president abruptly ordered the three outlets to be banned over “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”. The outlets swiftly sued over the move, which sparked widespread criticism from other news organizations and press freedom advocates.
In a legal filing earlier this week, Department of Justice lawyers argued that the ban was necessary for national security reasons, and listed examples of articles that relied on non-public information.
But Kelly was unswayed, and argued in his ruling that the way in the which the White House banned the organizations had likely violated due process protections for journalists – and well-established legal precedent set in two press access cases by the United States court of appeals for the District of Columbia.
“Plaintiffs are also likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process,” he wrote. “The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest.”
The judge said that, based on case law, before a press pass can be revoked, the White House “must promulgate rules or standards governing the conduct that would lead to such revocation. And the reporter must ‘receive fair notice not only of the conduct that would subject him to punishment, but also of the magnitude of the sanction that the White House might impose’.”
The three news organizations were not given advance notice that they were in violation of any set of standards and only received formal notice – in letters sent to each news organization on Tuesday – that they “exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”.
Michael Kenneth Velchik, a justice department attorney representing the Trump White House, argued that such a process had been laid out in the letters, which informed each news organization that they had until 5pm on Friday to contest the ban. (The letters said that if the organizations did not submit such a challenge, it would become final.)
But the judge said the standard mentioned in the letters was “so vague it hardly does the trick”, and concluded that even the defendants “do not dispute that plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked”.
The judge also wrote that he was “skeptical … that defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes”. He cited comments from Trump about how the ban was for content-based reasons.
A hearing for a preliminary injunction will be expedited to be held during the 14-day period in which the passes are returned, the judge said.
Theodore J Boutrous Jr, an attorney for CNN, MS Now and Politico, praised the judge’s determination. “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law,” he said in a statement. “We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
Seemingly anticipating a loss, Trump already said in a post on Truth Social earlier this week that the White House would appeal any adverse ruling.

articles.title_orig: Iran offers US new seven-day ceasefire proposal
articles.title_zh: Iran offers US new seven-day ceasefire proposal
articles.content_orig:
Country says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon
Iran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets.
The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed.
Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation.
Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal.
Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen.
Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making.
Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: “We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.”
He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump.
The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear program much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear program under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry.
Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal.
Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling.
For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait.
Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process.
Earlier in the day, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , met Araghchi, his Iranian counterpart, for the first time in New York.
It was also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year, and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.
Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.
He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran.
Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.
A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.
Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.
Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.”
Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.
He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.
Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”

articles.title_zh: How every senator voted on the Iran war powers resolution
articles.content_orig:
The Senate on Thursday narrowly voted down a measure demanding an end to the U.S. war with Iran .
The chamber voted 49-50 on the resolution, the latest to call for an end to the war.
All but four Republicans voted against the measure despite concerns that GOP candidates will face fallout in November's midterm elections from the war's economic costs. Some Republicans running in tight races have recently broken with President Donald Trump and called for an end to the war to bring gas prices down , a sign of potential voter discontent over the war's impact on the economy.
The Republicans who voted for the resolution were Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Maine's Susan Collins , Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky. Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the lone Democrat to vote against it.
Sen. Angela Alsobrooks , D-Md., did not vote despite having been in the Senate earlier Thursday. Alsobrooks has previously voted for similar resolutions. But if she had again voted that way on Thursday, the resolution still would have failed.
"Senator Alsobrooks has voted 13 times to end the war in Iran. Unfortunately, she was dealing with an urgent family matter during today's vote so was unable to cast her fourteenth vote to end the war in Iran," Alsobrooks' spokesperson Meredith Happy said in a statement to CNBC. "She believes every day that this war rages on, Americans are paying for it at the gas pump and the grocery store—and too many American service members have paid with their lives. She continues to urge this President to end this war once and for all."
An affirmative vote on the measure, known as a War Powers Resolution , would have directed Trump to remove U.S. troops from hostilities in Iran unless Congress explicitly approves the war.
The Senate has voted repeatedly on similar measures since the war began, approving one of them. The White House has effectively ignored that vote, arguing that the War Powers Act is unconstitutional.
The measure voted on Thursday, which like the one adopted was a so-called "concurrent resolution," did not carry the force of law and is never signed by the president, making the vote largely symbolic even if it had passed.
The Democratic leaders of the legislative push, however, argue that the Constitution vests authority to declare war in Congress, not the executive branch, and that the president must abide by their disapproval whether or not he signs it.
"The president right now is in violation of the Constitution and the War Powers Act and the concurrent resolution that we've already passed," said Sen. Tim Kaine , D-Va., who has led a number of the votes to end the war.
"We shouldn't have to do a second one because the president should follow the law, but we are doing a second one on the theory that maybe after a number of months more people will join us, the American public is even more deeply opposed to this war."
The measure cleared the House in July and faced just a 50-vote threshold to clear the Senate. Democrats have seen an uptick in Republican support in recent votes to end the war, as the administration has blown through timelines to seek congressional approval for the conflict.
The war has also created a challenging political environment for incumbent Republicans, who could lose control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections that loom less than six weeks away.
Gas prices, which have spiked throughout the conflict, currently average $4.48 per gallon nationwide, according to AAA . Recently, runaway diesel prices have begun stressing farmers and truckers and have alarmed Republicans in midwestern states, who have begun to distance themselves from the White House and call for an end to the war.
Lawmakers are set to hit the campaign trail for nearly all of October, and will need to explain to voters what they are doing to bring down prices.
"There are a lot of good things we can talk about; the problem is what you did for me recently doesn't even hardly count," said Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., when asked about how Republicans can message to economically anxious voters. "The other thing that we get to talk about ... is that at least we're not socialists."

New, mysterious and cryptic clips of Dakota Johnson flanked by another woman and man have taken rhe internet by storm, but this time, they aren’t part of her latest movie, “Verity”; they’re part of a Taylor Swift music video. Swift announced Thursday that she will unveil the music video for “ Patient Zero ” at the MTV VMAs on Sunday, and in the meantime,  gave Swifties a very short (13-second) sneak peek, revealing Johnson as one of the stars.
Johnson opened about her role in the video at the “Verity” red carpet premiere in London on Thursday.
“Working with your friends is like the most fun thing on the planet because we’ve known each other for so long, we respect each other’s creative minds, and to be able to work alongside her and support and assist and be a person whom she tells what to do is wonderful,” Johnson said.
Johnson emphasized her excitement on Ambar Lee and Leah Briars’ Fangirl Nation podcast on Thursday.
“Taylor and I have been friends for a really long time and we’re very close, and we decided to work together and it’s great,” Johnson said. “Normally I would say ‘Don’t work with your friends,’ but we work really well together. It was so fun. So fun. It was the best. We just had the best time.”
Their decades-long friendship was further confirmed with Johnson’s attendance at Swift’s star-studded wedding at Madison Square Garden this July.
Swift announced the single on Tuesday, followed by the news of “ The Life of a Showgirl : The Encore” on Wednesday. The album, an expanded version of last year’s “The Life of a Showgirl,” includes four new tracks: “Patient Zero,” “Cleveland!,” “Pink Clouding” and “Babylon.”
“About a year ago, you guys did a truly unfathomable thing,” Swift wrote on social media. “Something that completely blew my mind… You gave ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ the biggest first week for an album in history. I took a trip to Sweden to celebrate with Max and Shellback, my two collaborators on this album. Really, we just wanted to reflect and take in how grateful we were for the moment we were in, but there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: We wrote more songs. I hope you love them, because they were born out of pure gratitude for your exuberance for and celebration of the album we made. ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ including four new songs, is out on Friday and available to preorder and save now.”

articles.title_zh: California Supreme Court orders Riverside County sheriff to return 650,000 seized ballots
articles.content_orig:

SACRAMENTO — Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco got slapped down Thursday by the California Supreme Court in not one but two cases. Ouch.
First, the court told Bianco to return more than 600,000 ballots he had seized as part of an ill-conceived, conspiracy-laden “investigation” into voter fraud — making it clear it was the sheriff who was the criminal.
“The seizure of the ballots was unlawful,” the court wrote , before ordering Bianco to give them back to the registrar of voters and “refrain from further handling of the ballots except as necessary to comply with our order.”
Then the court, in a separate case , told Bianco he’s not a law unto himself, and in fact does have a boss in the form of the state Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta. Bonta had previously ordered Bianco to pause his investigation, and Bianco largely ignored him.
The court found that the constitutional authority held by the attorney general “includes the power to give binding directions to sheriffs .”
Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco confiscated ballots, claiming he was investigating election fraud. California’s Supreme Court justices called Bianco’s logic “bizarre.”
While the high-profile lawsuit about Bianco’s seizure of hundreds of thousands of ballots from last year’s special election on redistricting has grabbed headlines, the second case about the authority of the state attorney general to oversee all California sheriffs and district attorneys is equally powerful.
It’s the first time the court has weighed in on a long-running debate in California over whether elected sheriffs have to answer to anyone . Not only did Bianco lose for election deniers everywhere in the first case, he also managed to clarify for all California sheriffs in the second case that they are not as powerful as some would like to believe.
Combined, the two opinions by the state’s highest court give another layer of assurance to Golden State residents that the integrity of the November midterm elections is as secure as the state can make it — some welcome news in a national landscape where free and fair elections are increasingly at risk.
Before we get into what the ruling means for midterms in California, there are two overlooked bits that make these cases even more interesting.
First, gubernatorial candidate and former Atty. Gen. Xavier Becerra has been closely involved in the ballot-seizing case, but also pretty quiet about it.
Whenever a politician does something good and doesn’t advertise it, it always catches my attention. Politicians, especially ones running for office,  aren’t big on modesty.
But Becerra has not spent a lot of time talking about this, even though he is actually a working attorney on this case, as an advisor to the UCLA Voting Rights Project . He came up with ideas, he participated — this wasn’t just a put-my-name-on-it role, I’ve been told by folks who know.
And it’s not the first time Becerra has helped the Voting Rights Project in a major endeavor. It was their work that helped define the legal arguments that made Proposition 50 happen. That’s last year’s ballot initiative that redrew California voting maps to favor Democrats, in response to a Texas effort to gerrymander in favor of Republicans. It was Proposition 50 ballots that Bianco seized.
“Today the California Supreme Court handed voters a great victory,” Becerra said in a statement from the voting project. “The Court knocked election deniers off their feet and strengthened our hand in election protection just ahead of the November vote. We must use every lever at our disposal to beat back voter interference and intimidation.”
That line about knocking election deniers is not hyperbole. In some far-right, conspiracy-rich circles, Bianco’s cowboy-saving-the-day routine was viewed as heroic. Maybe even something to emulate.
Across the country, there are rumblings — including from President Trump — about seizing ballots from past or future elections. While this ruling is firmly rooted in California law, most states have similar chains of custody when it comes to ballots. So it’s likely to at least make other would-be-Biancos pause.
In a later interview, Becerra told me that the Voting Rights Project was “the one thing I decided I would do after I came home from being secretary in Washington, D.C.,” whether he ran for office or not, “just because I so believe in the work that they do.”
The state’s high court issued a ruling Thursday on whether Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco had the authority to seize more than half a million ballots in what the former Republican candidate for governor claimed was an investigation into voter fraud.
He said as he campaigns this year, he’s seeing anxiety in minority communities from that interference and intimidation, maybe even fear that could pressure some legal voters to sit this one out.
“It makes it tough when you’ve got all these things standing in your way before you even get to thinking about going to vote,” Becerra said. “The Latino community, other communities, mostly under-served communities, I always tell them, we’re not rich. The way we win these things is by voting.”
The second fact that caught my attention was a concurring opinion on the ballot case by Justice Goodwin Liu.
While the court was unanimous in its findings, Liu wrote his own opinion highlighting how the Riverside registrar of voters was “caught between a rock and a hard place” when the sheriff of his own county showed up with a warrant, guns and “enough trucks to remove several pallets of materials.”
That trifecta, Liu wrote, left the registrar little room for dissent — but that’s a problem.
Liu’s point seemed to be that with the current state of our president making election denial chic, our voting officials need to step up. He said the registrar should have come directly to the court for relief, and not left it to the Voting Rights Project and other plaintiffs.
“It is a lot to ask of our election officials that they not only do their jobs competently but also stand ready to sue anyone who unlawfully interferes with their duties,” Liu wrote. “Yet here we are.”
Since Bianco seized the ballots, state law has been changed. This session, legislators passed (and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed) at least 13 laws pertaining to election security, including making it a felony to break the chain of ballot custody, and ensuring that local election officials immediately contact the state in instances when that is threatened. Those laws will offer protection to election officials if a situation like this comes up again.
But Liu’s point is still valid. Being an election official is no longer a sleepy little job, but a front-line battle for democracy, and for “our democracy to flourish, our elections must be conducted in accordance with the law.”
Which brings us back to the midterms. California shouldn’t be complacent , but the state isn’t slouching on preparation, or resolve.
As Bonta put it, “if you can imagine it, we are ready for it.”
I’m not quite that confident — and definitely concerned for contests outside of the Golden State — but Thursday’s rulings are a reminder that the law still holds, even when lawmen try to break it.

articles.title_orig: Presidents Cup: Scottie Scheffler, Sam Burns sneak through tough opening round as U.S. takes early lead at Medinah
articles.title_zh: Presidents Cup: Scottie Scheffler, Sam Burns sneak through tough opening round as U.S. takes early lead at Medinah
articles.content_orig:
Nobody can legitimately question how good of a golfer Scottie Scheffler is. He's the top-ranked golfer in the world for a reason, and has absolutely dominated the PGA Tour over the last several years.
But Scheffler's struggles on the international stage, a trend he can't seem to shake, continued on Thursday at Medinah Country Club in Chicago.
Scheffler was in the opening group at the 2026 Presidents Cup on Thursday, playing alongside Sam Burns in the first of five four-ball matches against the International team. The two managed to sneak out a 1-up win over Min Woo Lee and Sungjae Im, thanks to a huge save at the 17th, to get the United States on the board. It was also the first Presidents Cup or Ryder Cup match that Burns and Scheffler have won playing together.
By the end of the day, the U.S. took a 3-2 lead over the International team ahead of the foursomes matches on Friday. They've led after the opening session in 12 of the 16 Presidents Cups.
"We just did our best to stay in it," Scheffler said. "I felt like both teams got off to pretty hot starts today and we cooled off a little bit off that."
Scheffler opened the day with a walk-in birdie. But that was about his only highlight. Lee and Im quickly tied the match back up as Scheffler struggled to get much of anything going. He missed the green at the short par-3 7th and hit his tee shot into the crowd, for example, and couldn't get many putts to fall the rest of the way.
That largely left Burns as the one to try and hold things down. He sank a big birdie putt at the 9th to keep the match tied as they made the turn, and Lee and Im missed three straight birdie looks of their own that would have given them their first lead of the day. They finally jumped ahead of Burns and Scheffler on the 13th after Scheffler missed a 3-footer for birdie, though Burns made a putt on the 14th to even things up once again.
Scheffler got a 4-foot par putt to fall on the 17th, while Im missed a similar look in a rough mistake, to finally put the Americans in the lead for good. Scheffler had to save par after landing in the bunker at the 18th, however, to avoid splitting the point.
Scheffler's record on the international stage is lagging behind his other accomplishments. He's got a 3-6-3 record at the Ryder Cup, and he entered this week with a 3-5-1 record in Presidents Cup matches. Scheffler has never won a Presidents Cup singles match, either, though he's 2-0-1 in those at the Ryder Cup.
Scheffler and Burns, who are very good friends off the course, were a combined 0-3-1 when paired together at the Ryder Cup and Presidents Cup before Thursday's win. Not great.
Luckily for Scheffler and the Americans, they're now in the lead after the first day in Chicago. Just not by much.
"I saw those guys competing their asses off out there," U.S. captain Brandt Snedeker said. "I'm really proud of them. A session win is a session win, we're going to take it any way we can get it. So happy for Scottie and Sam to go out there in that lead match and get that big win for us to lead us off.
"This is a long week. This is one session. We've got four more to go. Just proud of the way these guys started us off."
While the Scheffler-Burns group was slow, two pairs of Americans wasted no time in their matches behind them.
Justin Thomas and rookie Jackson Koivun rolled to a 4&3 win over Corey Conners and Nico Echavarria in the third match of the day. Koivun made three birdies on the front side to grab a lead almost immediately, and Koivun — who only made his PGA Tour debut mid-season earlier this year — looked comfortable out there.
Thomas then sank a birdie putt of his own from off the green at the 14th to push their lead back to three, which was enough to carry them to the early win. Thomas has now won his last seven four-ball matches at the Presidents Cup, which is tied for the all-time record. And at 21, Koivun is now the second-youngest American behind only Jordan Spieth to win a Presidents Cup match.
Wyndham Clark and Collin Morikawa cruised to a similar 3&2 win over Ryan Fox and Adam Scott. Clark went 4-under on the front nine himself, which was more than enough to keep Fox and Scott at bay. Clark then pushed their lead to three with a birdie on the 15th, which allowed them to end the match on the following hole.
Scott is playing in his 12th career Presidents Cup, and Thursday was his 55th overall match, both of which tied the all-time record with Phil Mickelson.
While they were in the last and slowest group of the day, Tom Kim and Si Woo Kim had little issue getting past Chris Gotterup and Patrick Cantlay, winning 3&2 to secure an easy point for the Internationals.
They went 2-up through their first two holes to take control of the match almost instantly. While Cantlay and Gotterup rallied briefly — they made three birdies in a four-hole stretch to tie things up — that was all they could do. Cantlay became a non-factor the rest of the way while Kim and Kim easily pushed their lead to three before taking the win. Si Woo's birdie at the 14th was from distance, too, and banked in perfectly.
Tom nearly had a hole-in-one at the 16th and actually banked his ball off the flag stick. That would have been the third ace in Presidents Cup history.
Hideki Matsuyama and Ryo Hisatsune, meanwhile, took off on the back nine to grab their 3&1 win. After hanging in a battle on the front nine, the pair won back-to-back holes before making the turn to take control of the match while Xander Schauffele and Cameron Young struggled to get putts to fall. Eventually, after Young missed a birdie look at the 17th, Matsuyama and Hisatsune were able to put the Internationals on the board for the first time all day.
The two teams will return to Medinah on Friday for five foursomes, or alternate shot, matches.

articles.title_orig: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by February, study suggests
articles.title_zh: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by February, study suggests
articles.content_orig:
Nearly half a million people across the world could lose their lives by February due to El Niño-driven extreme heat, according to a sobering new report.
El Niño, a natural climate pattern which typically ramps up global temperature, has now crossed into super-sized territory and is on its way to becoming record-breakingly strong.
Combined with the global warming the planet is already experiencing from fossil fuel pollution, the heat consequences could be devastating, according to the analysis from the Climate Impact Lab, a team of scientists, economists and data engineers headquartered at the University of Chicago, and published Wednesday.
Heat is the most deadly form of extreme weather - although heat deaths are not well-tracked, even in rich nations. The report estimates the heat from El Niño could take 451,000 lives between June 2026, when it arrived, and February 2027. Those deaths would be in addition to the usual number of heat-related deaths.
The researchers believe this number is likely to rise - El Nino is expected to last until the Northern Hemisphere spring, meaning its heat impacts will linger into the summer months.
The deaths from extreme heat would also come in addition to those expected from other El Niño-fueled extreme weather, including fires, floods and droughts, according to the report.
The report has not yet been peer-reviewed but uses peer-reviewed methodology to reach its conclusions.
"We have long been able to predict the impacts of temperatures on crops, and now we can predict their impact on the worst outcome - death," said Michael Greenstone, a report author, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and an economics professor at the University of Chicago.
"This is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbors, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives," he added.
Scientists project that El Niño will push global land temperatures up 1.2 degrees Celsius (2.1 Fahrenheit) above normal in the coming months. This unusual warmth is exactly what climate change is projected to bring in 20 years time, and will lead to 44% more days of extreme heat than would be expected in a normal year, according to the study.
The current El Niño is a "postcard from our future" that's arriving before the world's had time to adapt, the authors write.
The regions expected to be most affected are overwhelmingly in the Global South. The report identifies Nigeria as where the most El Niño heat deaths are expected, with a projected 31,400 lives lost. Other countries at high risk include Indonesia, Sudan, India and Brazil. The United States is also in the top 20 affected countries, with a projected 3,500 deaths.
The report combined peer-reviewed methods on the relationship between temperature and mortality in more than 24,000 regions across the world and seasonal temperature forecasts. The death projections were compared to the same months of an average year between 1996 and 2025.
Raquel Nunes, associate professor in health and environment at the University of Warwick in England, who was not involved in the report, said "the estimate of 451,000 deaths is plausible as a modeling exercise, but it should not be viewed as a definitive prediction. Its value lies in highlighting the potentially severe consequences of El Niño-driven extreme heat and the urgent need for preparedness."
The study is currently awaiting peer-review, but the scientists said they released the shorter report first due to El Nino's rapid strengthening. "Given that there is still time now for policymakers and others to take action to prevent these deaths, we felt our findings couldn't wait for the peer review process to play out. That would certainly be too late to act for this El Niño cycle," said a Climate Impact Lab spokesperson.
Measures countries can take include early heat warnings, health action plans, ensuring cooling and hydration centers are available and expanding healthcare coverage, the report says.
"Increasing emergency response and better targeting our efforts can save many lives this year," said report co-author Tamma Carleton, faculty head of research for the Climate Impact Lab and an assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley. "But 20 years from now, once today's extreme temperatures become the new normal, we don't want to be in a constant state of emergency."

articles.title_orig: Inside the Bombshell Article That Inspired ‘Primetime’
articles.title_zh: Inside the Bombshell Article That Inspired ‘Primetime’
articles.content_orig:
Senior Entertainment Writer
Nearly 20 years ago, Luke Dittrich received an email inquiring about his interest in reporting out a story about Chris Hansen and To Catch a Predator . He had never seen the show and was unaware of the fatal incident that spurred the note: The suicide of assistant district attorney Bill Conradt, who’d been caught by the watchdog group and Dateline NBC partner Perverted Justice in expressing sexual interest in an adult posing as a 13-year-old boy. He killed himself just as the show’s camera crew was planning to enter his home in Murphy, Texas, for what was supposed to be in line with Predator ’s tradition of filming sting operations in real time. Dittrich’s task would be to report out what could lead to such a harrowing tragedy taking place on a popular TV show — and the resulting article, “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” unfurled that and more.
A New York Times best-selling and National Magazine Award-winning writer, Dittrich had spoken to To Catch a Predator ’s infamous host, Chris Hansen, in what he now describes as a “contentious” conversation that plays out in the longform article’s final section. He had all but lived inside his mind for months, through several trips to Texas and a submerging into the dark, complex web of the Conradt case and the true-crime phenomenon that surrounded it. And then, once his piece was published, he moved onto other stories. He did not follow Predator ’s short-lived run from there, where Hansen’s career went, or how the show lived on in ways no one could have predicted.
And then he got another call a few years ago, inquiring about the rights to his article, which were available. This all led to Primetime , Lance Oppenheim ’s fever dream of a film which dramatizes the world of To Catch a Predator and builds toward the show’s misbegotten trip to Texas. (It hits theaters via A24 on Friday.) Robert Pattinson portrays Hansen in an at times uncanny, at other times wildly impressionistic performance, working off of a script by debut screenwriter Ajon Singh that is entirely its own creation, while sharing key DNA with the article on which it’s based.
It’s been a surreal moment for Dittrich, then, returning to a world he’d long left behind as, more than anything else, a casual observer. In conversation with The Hollywood Reporter , he speaks about visiting the set, his memories of Hansen at the time, and how his perspective on what he wrote about has changed in the time since.
So you’re approached by Esquire with the idea for a longform story on To Catch a Predator , coming off of the tragedy in Texas. What was your relationship to the show at that point?
The thing was, I’d never watched an episode of To Catch a Predator . I hadn’t been following the news that closely. I was at the time living a pretty isolated life, up in the Yukon Territory. I had a toddler-aged daughter. When that email came in, I was actually down in Chile on my way to run a marathon in Antarctica for another story. I had a lot going on and wasn’t watching much TV.
I got on my laptop and started watching archived episodes of To Catch a Predator and found it, like most people do, extremely compelling television. But there was also something just sort of unusual and dark and strange about it. I basically then instantly begged Dave Katz [then an editor at Esquire , now editorial director of The Hollywood Reporter ] to let me go down to Dallas as soon as I got back from Antarctica, which is what I did. I spent two long reporting trips in and around Dallas while working on the story. They were amazing and memorable reporting trips for me.
Some highlights were just sitting in a motel room one afternoon furiously trying to figure out how to work this DVD burner that I had bought at the local Circuit City in order to make copies of a bunch of raw footage from NBC that I had gotten from a source and needed to return to the source as soon as possible. I remember sitting in another motel room with this tough, brilliant police detective named Gator who had been actively involved in what played out in Texas. In the middle of our interview, as he’s going through his role in the events, he just began sobbing…. I remember walking through the house that is featured at the end of the movie and just trying to steep in it.
And then as often happens, you move on to other stories. I finished writing the article, it came out, I talked about it a little bit, and then I sort of put it aside and I certainly had never been following the evolution of Chris Hansen’s career. I’d occasionally hear that he had talked smack about the article in some podcast, but I wasn’t really paying attention.
When did Hansen and To Catch a Predator come back into your orbit, via the movie?
It was less than four years ago, maybe three and a half years ago or so. I got another email out of the blue from a producer at Range, William Iannaccone, who said, “Hey, I read this article of yours about To Catch a Predator and I loved it and I just wanted to know if the rights were available.” I got on the phone with him and he was super smart and had this clear vision for it and seemed extremely driven to make something happen. I’d had conversations with producers like that before, about other stories, and usually nothing ends up happening. But this one, I sold the rights, I crossed my fingers, and then lo and behold.
Had there been any adaptation interest, or stops and starts, beforehand? Since we’re approaching 20 years since it was published.
I don’t really want to go into any specifics about it. At some points I’d gotten certain inquiries, and I also consulted on the documentary, Predators , which I think speaks to the enduring interest of this moment in history. Primetime and my article share DNA, but they’re completely different animals in a lot of ways. But I’m thrilled and proud to be associated with Primetime in any way because it’s just a super powerful piece of work.
Through your reporting of the article, what was your read on Chris Hansen at the time?
The tough thing for me about that question — and it’s a legitimate and it’s a good question — is that I put my feelings all on the page. What makes him an interesting character is he’s a complicated character and it’s very hard to summarize in a sentence or two what makes him so interesting, but he is indelible and so is the show. The show is operating on various levels and it’s catering to various kinds of appetites that we have as humans. But I’m a lousy critic. It’s a struggle for me to figure out what makes something good or powerful. I can just engage with it with my feelings and go from there.
I don’t have anything particularly pithy to say about Chris Hansen. He clearly was an interesting character to me, but more than that, what drew me to the story was just the tick-tock narrative of what played out during that moment in history. That’s one of the things that’s fascinating when I think about how Lance and Ajon and the whole cast and crew of Primetime were coming to this story. When I was working on my article, I was in this sort of little time capsule restricted by the boundaries of that particular place in time. I couldn’t see over the horizon in terms of the ripple effects that event may or may not have had.
What were the biggest challenges in reporting the story out?
You spend a lot of time trying to convince people to open up to you. Some of the people that ended up being my central sources for the story — I approached them in the first days of being on the ground in Texas, and they refused to talk to me, refused to talk to me, refused to talk to me until I talked to a whole bunch of other people that had been in their orbit. They got through them some sense of my approach to the story and realized that maybe he’s sort of okay to talk to. On my second trip back to Texas, the doors began to open for me. That’s not atypical with this sort of story, but it’s one thing that stands out.

OXFORD, Miss. — The two University of Mississippi students found dead under suspicious circumstances in recent days have been identified by the school — which also said the names were being released with their families' approval.
Robert Strang, a 20-year-old from Atlanta, is the older of the two victims. The second student was as Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old freshman from Colorado.
"We are heartbroken by the loss of our dear son and are trying to process this unimaginable loss," Strang's family spokesman Scott Sayres told Fox News Digital Thursday. "We are deeply grateful for the incredible outpouring of love, prayers and support by so many beloved friends and family. Their kindness has meant more to our family than we can ever express."
Hamilton's family said in a statement that "Aidan was a bright, wonderful young man who was taken too soon. He is greatly missed. We thank everyone for their prayers and support and ask that you respect our family’s privacy during this time of great loss."
Both families have asked for privacy and compassion as they mourn the losses of their sons.
TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS
Robert Strang pictured in an undated family photo. The 20-year-old University of Mississippi junior died under suspicious circumstances. (Strang family)
Separately, Commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Public Safety Sean Tindell told Fox News Digital that while authorities haven't uncovered any indications of foul play, they haven't ruled it out either.
"Until the autopsy is reported, and the investigators have an opportunity to get statements and collect evidence, then that final determination will not be made until later," he said.
Without the toxicology reports, it's also too early to determine whether kratom or other drugs were involved in the deaths. Police previously said that they found packages of kratom, which is commercially available in many places but not Lafayette County, at both scenes.
He also said that both deaths happened at around the same time, or at least within a few hours, which was also suspicious. However, he said he expects the autopsy reports to give investigators a more specific window.
"The timing of it is suspicious, but I don't know that they have any direct relation other than if they both had ingested the substance from the same source," he said. "Then at some point we would try to track it back to that source and take appropriate action."
Stewart Hall, a dorm building on the University of Mississippi campus where an 18-year-old student is believed to have died on Monday. Dispatch records show first responders arrived within a minute of being sent to the address. (Adam Sabes/Fox News Digital)
Social media posts from the Ole Miss chapter of the Phi Delta Theta fraternity identify Strang as one of seven co-chairmen of the 2026 Rush, when new members are recruited.
"As our university community continues to mourn the recent tragic loss of two of our students, I encourage everyone to remember that at the center of this are two grieving families, who are processing the unimaginable loss of a child," the school's Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Dr. Shawnboda Mead said in a statement Thursday afternoon.
"We have been in touch with the families to offer our deepest sympathies and share university support and resources. Until now, we have upheld their wishes not to release the names of their students," she continued. "Today, the families of Aidan Hamilton, a freshman from Englewood, Colo., and Robert Strang, a junior from Atlanta, have given us permission to share their names. The families have asked for privacy as they grieve."
Mead continued to urge the public not to rely on speculation or unverified information about the case as law enforcement continues to investigate both deaths.
"We offer heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and classmates of Aidan and Robert," she said. "While there are no words that can alleviate the tremendous sorrow they are experiencing, please keep them close in your thoughts and prayers during this time of immense grief."
Phi Delta Theta's Ole Miss chapter also put out a statement after the university, asking for prayers for both victims.
"Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them."

Strang was discovered at an off-campus home, according to the Lafayette County Coroner's Office. Hamilton, 18, is believed to have been found at Stewart Hall, a male dorm on the Ole Miss campus.

Authorities found packages of kratom , a commercially available drug that has been derided as "gas station heroin," at both scenes, however its role in either death was not immediately clear. articles.title_orig: US mortgage rates top 7% for first time in 20 months
articles.title_zh: US mortgage rates top 7% for first time in 20 months
articles.content_orig:
Increase comes after Fed decision to raise interest rates, as Americans struggle with high prices and stagnant wages
US mortgage rates surpassed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac, aggravating a housing market that has endured years of high interest rates and low supply.
The increase comes after the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates , which directly affect mortgage rates, for the first time since 2023, citing high inflation.
Rates on 16 September went up by a quarter of a point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. In new projections, a majority of the Fed’s rate-setting committee predicted at least one additional rate hike before the end of this year.
Last year, the Freddie Mac 30-year-mortgage rate, commonly used on home loans across the country, had been trending down from 7.79% – a generational high reached in late 2023.
But rates have been creeping back up since late February, when the US and Israel launched its war with Iran . The conflict drove inflation to its highest levels in three years and sharply increased energy prices.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, topped $105 earlier on Thursday.
after newsletter promotion
On Thursday, the 10-year US treasury yield – which underpins the 30-year mortgage rate and other borrowing costs – also reached its highest level since July 2007 and the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its peak since 2004 as investors raised expectations for another Fed rate hike next month.
Earlier in September, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the Treasury would triple its buyback of government debt, but yields have continued to rise.
The housing market has long been in a slowdown, said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com , with existing home sales hitting their 2026 low so far in August and pending sales that have turned negative year over year.
“A 7% handle is as much psychological as mathematical, and it arrives at the point in the season when leverage usually shifts toward buyers,” said Smith.
High mortgage rates are just one of the many reasons why Americans are struggling to attain home ownership. Wages have not kept pace with higher inflation, and everyday costs are higher.
The frustration is expected to show up in November’s midterm elections as Republicans struggle to maintain control of Congress. Nearly three-quarters of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, according to a recent CNN poll conducted by SSRS , and two-thirds of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important” to their vote.

UNITED NATIONS — Saudi Arabia's foreign minister warned Thursday that the growing threat from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis extends far beyond his country's borders, calling for international cooperation to protect critical shipping routes after Saudi forces intercepted six ballistic missiles launched toward the kingdom.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud told Fox News Digital that Riyadh was coordinating with Washington and other international partners as Houthi attacks threatened Saudi territory and commercial shipping in the Red Sea.
The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday that its air defenses had intercepted six ballistic missiles allegedly launched by the Houthis toward the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu, according to Reuters. It was not immediately clear whether the attacks caused casualties or damage.
AMERICANS WARNED AGAIN TO RETHINK TRAVEL AS MISSILE ATTACK RATTLES HISTORIC REGION
Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al-Saud and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, co-chairs of a United Nations high-level international conference hosted by France and Saudi Arabia to work towards a two-state solution between Israel and the Palestinians, listen to a question during a press briefing at U.N. headquarters in New York City, July 28, 2025. Saudi authorities also issued emergency warnings across several areas, including Jeddah and Mecca, before announcing that the immediate danger had passed. Yanbu, a major Red Sea oil export hub, has become particularly important as the war with Iran disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz .
Asked by Fox News Digital whether Saudi Arabia was receiving the support it needed from the US following reports that President Donald Trump had declined Saudi requests for direct military intervention against the Houthis, Prince Faisal emphasized the kingdom's ability to defend itself while calling for a broader international response.
"So we are, of course, defending ourselves. And we are responding as necessary to the attacks by the Houthis. But we are also, of course, coordinating with all of our international allies, because this is not just about Saudi Arabia," he said.

The foreign minister thanked countries already working with Riyadh and confirmed that discussions with Washington were continuing.
"And we are obviously continuing to work with our partners in the U.S., to address the issue of this conflict as well," he said.

In 2024, Microsoft and Qualcomm kicked off a new category of Windows hardware it called "Copilot+ PCs" that set the baseline for a new wave of AI-first computers, and launched with exclusive features that would not be made available on PCs that didn't meet a new set of system requirements.
The launch didn't go smoothly. Copilot+ PCs were met with immediate backlash from security researchers after discovering that Copilot+ PCs blockbuster feature, Recall, was woefully insecure. This forced the company to delay Recall and ship this new category of devices without its leading AI experience.
This pretty much tarnished the Copilot+ PC brand, and over the last two years more and more OEMs have dropped the moniker from marketing materials and product names. In fact, even Microsoft has seemingly stopped mentioning it.
I've noticed that none of the Surface PCs launched in 2026 include the Copilot+ PC moniker in their product names, unlike the Surface PCs that launched in 2025 and before. Now, you have to go digging to find any mention of Copilot+ compatibility in specification sheets.
At this year's Snapdragon Summit, I had the chance to ask Surface CVP Brett Ostrum about the lack of Copilot+ PC branding on its recent Surface PCs , and he confirmed that " these are not called Copilot+ PCs. They do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are. We still lean into the narrative around AI on the edge and being able to have a hybrid solution out there."
I've also asked Qualcomm's SVP of compute, Kedar Kondap, about his thoughts on the usage of the Copilot+ PC branding. He told me that "the purpose for Copilot+ PCs was to be able to deliver [NPU] experiences. So it was to define a certain category of devices with a certain bar and metric, like for example, a 45 TOPS NPU ... So from that perspective, it's more offering the same experiences, probably without just using [Copilot+ PC] terminology now. "
It's also worth mentioning that NVIDIA hasn't gone anywhere near the Copilot+ PC brand for its upcoming RTX Spark platform, even though all RTX Spark PCs meet the Copilot+ PC specification bar. I suspect that's a deliberate decision.
It seems pretty obvious that the Copilot+ PC brand hasn't resonated with the market, and OEMs and Microsoft itself are now quietly pulling back on that branding. The specification baseline for Copilot+ PC experiences still exists, it just no longer has a pretty marketing name tied to it.
The rough launch of Copilot+ PCs, paired with the fact that Microsoft Copilot itself doesn't have a very strong reputation these days, likely contributed to the decision to slowly retire the Copilot+ PC branding. The brand never made sense to me anyway... these PCs have nothing to do with Copilot.

At Meta’s annual developer conference today, the company announced its next VR Start Developer Competition, this time slated to award a prize pool of $1 million to spark the community to get cracking on Meta VR Glasses-compatible content.
Meta is hoping to appeal to developers of both new and existing projects across entertainment, gaming, and productivity.
Notably, if developers are submitting games, they’ll be considering submissions in genres that work well for seated play, without controllers, such as puzzle, strategy, casual, social, and narrative experiences.
Games must be “fully usable with hands, end-to-end,” Meta says, noting that Touch controller support is welcome, but not required.
“For a small team without a marketing budget, that visibility drives traffic to your Store listing and gives you something concrete to point to when you pitch a new project or recruit collaborators,” Meta says.
This comes ahead of the company’s Meta VR Glasses announced at Connect this week, which does support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, but doesn’t ship with them, instead putting its onboard hand and eye-tracking as its preferred control scheme.
Those are set to arrive sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300. Check out our hands-on with Meta VR Glasses to learn more .
The competition takes place from today until November 18th, 2026, and is offering up prizes ranging in value from $20,000 to $100,000 for successful submissions. Winners will be announced on or around December 11th, 2026.
Since Meta VR Glasses run the same operating system as Quest, developers can prototype on Quest 3 in addition to using platform simulators like Meta XR Simulator ( Unity | Unreal ), Meta Spatial Simulator , and Immersive Web Emulator⁠ .
Interested developers can join the Start program now to enter for competition.

It’s confirmed: The mysterious Motorola phone getting support for the privacy-focused GrapheneOS will be the Motorola Signature 27 that was announced earlier this week.
GrapheneOS, a privacy-focused take on Android that’s grown popular in recent years, has so far only been available on Pixel devices. That’s for a number of reasons relating back to how Google handles the software and the security components in Pixel (and Tensor) hardware.
But, now, GrapheneOS is officially stepping beyond Pixel and into a device that will come pre-loaded with its version of Android. It was announced that this would be a Motorola device, but which device was left a mystery as all existing Motorola devices were not compatible with the platform.
Unsurprisingly, though, the first GrapheneOS device from Motorola will be the Motorola Signature 27. GrapheneOS confirmed the news on Twitter/X , though other details are still minimal. It’s apparently still planned that devices will be sold with GrapheneOS pre-installed. The Signature 27 was announced earlier this week and its use of the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset is likely a major part of the reason it will be able to run GrapheneOS properly.
An exact release date for the Motorola Signature 27 has yet to be confirmed, and it’s unclear if GrapheneOS will be available right away either. It’s already known that future versions of Razr flip and Razr Fold will also support the privacy-focused OS.

Little more than an hour before a judge was set to hold a Thursday morning hearing approving the settlement agreement between Paramount and the attorneys general in the antitrust suit, a judge has granted a last-ditch emergency motion filed by the members of the grassroots Block the Merger coalition.
In an amicus brief motion, Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted the emergency motion and gave the parties a hard deadline of no later than 12:01 a.m. tomorrow morning to get everything in place. Today’s 11 a.m. hearing is still in place as of this moment.
The organizations Free Press, the Committee for the First Amendment, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, the Future Film Coalition, and the International Documentary Association all said in a joint statement, “The consent decree the state AGs agreed to in a backroom deal is weak, unenforceable, and leaves workers, journalists, and consumers in the dust. The settlement fails to address the grave dangers this merger poses — and no amount of spin can change that. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín’s ruling will allow the public to weigh in on this important issue and ensure the interests of those who will actually pay the price for the Ellisons’ sweetheart deal that the AGs failed to adequately represent are heard. We look forward to explaining that in further detail in our brief due at midnight tonight.”
Block the Merger in its filing from earlier today called the settlement deal from California AG Rob Bonta bad “for the future of film, entertainment, independent journalism, and a strong democracy in this country,” and in a statement today members of Block the Merger called Bonta’s deal “weak and unenforceable.” Members of the group earlier this week were protesting outside Paramount headquarters in Hollywood following the surprise settlement news.
“Hundreds of thousands of people across the country called on state attorneys general to enforce the law and to protect consumers, workers and free speech,” said Free Press Co-CEO Jessica J. González, who serves as co-counsel on the motion. “The weak and unenforceable deal the AGs struck with Paramount leaves us in the lurch. We deserve our day in court.”
“We believe the consent decree fails to meaningfully address or mitigate the harms that will be caused by this monopoly merger to the entertainment industry, diverse storytelling, independent filmmaking, consumer interests, a free press, First Amendment rights, and fundamentally, democracy,” stated Mara Verheyden-Hilliard, Steering Committee for the Committee for the First Amendment and First Amendment litigator. “It does not serve to benefit anyone except the owner family of Paramount and those holding political power who will use this corporate consolidation as a proxy force for First Amendment suppression of disfavored expression and viewpoints.”
Paramount did not respond to a request for comment.
The settlement agreement, which was reached on Monday, September 21, required that Paramount commit to concessions for a period of five years , with some of the concessions being that if it failed to meet its promised 30 movies released annually, it would be forced to divest its stake in Miramax and it would have to pay $30 million to a fund for Hollywood union members. It was also required to keep some of the same theatrical terms during the duration of the settlement, it would have to negotiate Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery cable channels as separate entities, and it agreed to spend an extra $1.5 billion annually on production in the United States. It also required a panel of journalists to be put in place to maintain the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News.
Block the Merger saw the deal as toothless, as it didn’t force any divestitures, and it didn’t assure that production dollars would be spent in California specifically.
The timing of this hail mary motion is significant because Paramount needs to begin paying a ticking fee of several million dollars a day to WBD shareholders for every day past October 1 the deal fails to close. With the settlement reached, the hope was that this would be closed within a matter of weeks.
